the percentile bootstrap 95% CI for the risk difference was [-0.49, 0.30] pp, includes zero, p=0.69, not statistically significant
the bias-corrected bootstrap 95% CI for the risk difference was [0.19, 0.61] pp, excluding zero

sensitivity analyses showed consistent positive associations across models (ORs 1.19-1.30) with p-values ranging 0.028-0.068
the overall hypothesis conclusion is 'not supported' because the primary estimand is inconclusive and the evidence is contradictory

the evidence is judged not to overwhelmingly support the hypothesis, given the rare event rate (1.25%), substantial bootstrap bias (z0=1.70), and wide confidence intervals relative to the point estimate, and the small absolute effect magnitude (0.26pp)

spans.note: separator, Section 3 heading, Unit of Analysis subheading

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad, with each observation representing counts of interactions (games together, cards received) for a unique pair
99,645 total dyads were analyzed
83,655 dyads (84%) were light skin, defined as skin tone rating ≤0.25
15,990 dyads (16%) were dark skin, defined as skin tone rating ≥0.75
1,241 dyads had at least one red card, a 1.25% event rate
light-skin dyads had 1,016 red-card events (1.21%)
dark-skin dyads had 225 red-card events (1.41%)
there were 1,214 unique players (1,015 light-skinned, 199 dark-skinned)
there were 2,768 unique referees
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded due to missing skin tone ratings because players lacked photos
7,961 dyads were excluded due to missing covariate data (position, height, weight)
38,422 dyads with medium skin tone (0.25<rating<0.75) were excluded to create a clear contrast between light and dark groups
the outcome variable used was a binary indicator of whether any red card was received in the dyad
the original variable was a count of red cards (range 0-2) but was converted to binary due to the extreme rarity of multiple red cards
the exposure variable was a binary indicator of dark skin (≥0.75) versus light skin (≤0.25, reference group)
skin tone was measured by two independent raters who categorized players from profile photos on a 5-point scale (1='very light' to 5='very dark'), later normalized to 0-1
inter-rater reliability was excellent (r=0.92)
scores were averaged between the two raters
log(games), the natural log of the number of games in the dyad, was included as a covariate to adjust for exposure opportunity
games was log-transformed to account for diminishing marginal effects
player position (12 categories) was adjusted for as a potential confounder, since certain positions may receive more cards due to tactical roles and position distributions differ by skin tone

league country (4 categories: England, France, Germany, Spain) was adjusted for to account for different refereeing standards and league cultures, noting distribution differs substantially by skin tone
a logistic regression model was fitted: logit(P(red card)) = β0 + β1(dark_skin) + β2(log_games) + β3(position) + β4(league)

marginal standardization was used to calculate the risk difference by generating predicted probabilities twice (dark_skin=0, then dark_skin=1) holding other covariates at observed values, and taking the mean difference
each player appears in multiple dyads (mean=82 dyads per player), creating within-player correlation
cluster-robust standard errors, clustered by player, were used to account for this non-independence

bootstrap confidence intervals for the risk difference were obtained via cluster bootstrap at the player level with 200 iterations, and both percentile and BCa CIs were reported due to detected bias in the bootstrap distribution
games was log-transformed because it is continuous and right-skewed
a binary indicator for skin tone was created from the continuous 0-1 scale
the outcome was converted to binary from the count variable of red cards
no sampling weights were applied; all dyads were weighted equally
no player or referee fixed effects were used
clustering was addressed via robust standard errors rather than within-player/referee estimation, because the primary interest is between-player skin-tone variation
all sensitivity analyses showed a consistent positive direction of effect, with varying statistical significance
a minimal model (games only) yielded coefficient 0.183, SE 0.088, OR 1.20, 95% CI [1.01,1.43], p=0.038
a model without position adjustment yielded coefficient 0.175, SE 0.096, OR 1.19, 95% CI [0.99,1.44], p=0.20
a continuous skin-tone model yielded OR 1.30, 95% CI [1.03,1.64], p=0.028
the continuous-model OR represents the change in odds per 1-unit increase in skin tone rating (very light to very dark)
adding position adjustment increases the coefficient, suggesting position acts as a negative confounder (suppressor variable)
dark-skinned players are more likely to play attacking positions (forwards, wingers), which receive fewer cards than defensive positions
after adjusting for position, the skin-tone effect becomes stronger
the continuous skin-tone model shows a dose-response relationship, strengthening the case for causal interpretation
14.7% of dyads were excluded due to missing skin tone ratings, because photos were unavailable for 467 of 2,053 players

spans.assertion: raters were blind to the research question, though aware they were rating skin tone, which could introduce social desirability bias
despite excellent inter-rater reliability (r=0.92), categorizing into binary light/dark loses information
red cards are rare events (1.25%), leading to wide confidence intervals, instability in risk-difference estimation, and potential small-sample bias despite large N
multiple red cards per dyad are extremely rare (only 25 dyads with 2 red cards), limiting the ability to model counts
the controlled confounders were position, league country, and games (exposure)
player behavior/aggression was not directly measured; goals and yellow cards served as imperfect proxies
referee characteristics were not used in the primary model (country-level bias measures were available but unused), and referee identity was not controlled via fixed effects
team tactics and playing style were not controlled for
player reputation/history beyond the dyad was not controlled for
game importance, score, and timing were not available and thus not controlled for
implicit bias variation across referees was assumed homogeneous within country rather than modeled as varying

position is judged more likely a confounder than a mediator, since it likely has strong non-discriminatory determinants (physical attributes, skill set), despite the possibility that adjusting for it over-controls if skin tone affects position assignment
the 1.25% event rate leads to large bootstrap bias (z0=1.70), disagreement between percentile and bias-corrected CIs, and different conclusions from OR vs RD
with only 225 red-card events in the dark-skinned group, the estimates are unstable
each player appears in about 82 dyads on average (about 3 games per dyad)

clustering was addressed via robust standard errors, but residual dependence may remain, player-specific propensities are not fully accounted for, and referee-specific tendencies are not modeled except via league
the data covers European male professional soccer only, for the 2012-2013 season

the analyst approached the analysis with strong skepticism, as instructed, expecting to disconfirm the hypothesis
